headlines.title: Bay Area voter guide: What to know about the November 2026 election
headlines.description: What to Know — Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026 California will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. Voters will decide 14 state propositions. Regional sales tax Measure RTM, the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, aims to increase funds for public transit. California’s Congressional District 11 race features Scott Wiener and Connie Chan competing to succeed Nancy Pelosi. Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez will face off again after a special election in August where Wahab secured victory to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. All 80 California Assembly seats are up for reelection, as well as 20 Senate seats. California’s general election is Nov. 3, with statewide races and propositions as well as key local races and measures across the Bay Area. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot, including important dates and deadlines, how to register or check your status, where and when to vote, and what’s on the ballot. In this guide: Key election dates Check voter registration status How to register to vote How to find your polling place What to bring to your polling place How to track your mail-in ballot Why is California choosing a new governor? 14 California propositions What to watch Alameda County What to watch Contra Costa County What to watch Napa County What to watch San Francisco What to watch San Mateo County What to watch Santa Clara County What to watch Solano County County election offices Key election dates The last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 general election is Oct. 19. County election officials will start mailing ballots by Oct. 5. Ballot drop-off locations open on Oct. 6 Last day to register to vote for the general election is Oct. 19. First vote centers open for early in-person voting in all Voter’s Choice Act counties on Oct. 24. In person early voting locations in the state open on Oct. 31. Election Day, Nov. 3, is the last day to vote in-person or return a ballot by 8 p.m. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked no later than Nov. 3. If mailing on election day, get a hand-stamped postmark from a postal employee inside a post office. Visit the California Secretary of State’s website for a full list of key dates and deadlines. Check voter registration status Voters can check their registration at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov to confirm their mailing address and voting status. How to register to vote California residents can register to vote in elections at registertovote.ca.gov. Note Oct. 19 is the last day to register for the general election. Same day voter registration window will be open from Oct. 20 up to the Nov. 3 election day. Visit caearlyvoting.sos.ca.gov for a list of early voting locations to complete same day registration. How to find your polling place Visit the California Secretary of State’s website, where you can input your address to find your polling location and see what is on your ballot. Voters can also visit their county elections office for more information. Scroll down to the Bay Area county election offices section of this guide for further contact information. What to bring to your polling place Voters usually are not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot, according to the Secretary of State’s website. There are some instances when providing identification is required: Voting for the first time after registering to vote by mail and did not provide a driver license number California identification number or the last four digits of social security number are missing on registration form In these cases voters should plan to bring identification to a polling place or bring a copy of it with their vote-by-mail ballot. The Secretary of State says the following are acceptable forms of identification: Passport Driver license Official state identification card Student identification card Copy of recent utility bill Sample ballot booklet received from county elections office Any document received by a government agency How to track your mail-in ballot Voters can track their vote-by-mail ballot and confirm it has been received by using the state’s Where’s My Ballot? tool at california.ballottrax.net/voter/. Ballots mailed in may take a few days to appear on the website. Why is California choosing a new governor? Gov. Gavin Newsom terms out after this year and voters will choose between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years. He also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. What are the 14 California propositions voters will decide in the November election? Here’s a list of the California propositions on the November ballot. Use the expandable graphic below for a breakdown on what to know about each measure. 2026 California Ballot Propositions Click on a proposition to see more information about what will happen if it does or doesn’t pass. Source: NBC Staff Reports • Interactive: Annetta Stogniew Regional measure to watch Measure RTM: The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Races and measures to watch in Alameda County California Congressional District 14: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez will face off again to determine who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab topped Hernandez in an August special election to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. Swalwell resigned from Congress earlier this year after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. District 14 includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore. Measure X in Berkeley: Would establish 10% limit on annual rent increases and other changes to the city’s rent ordinance. Measure Y in Berkeley: Parcel tax to pay for arts projects. Measure Z in Berkeley: Parcel tax to fund a public bank. Measure AA in Berkeley: Increase soda tax Measure EE in Oakland: Shift city to a strong mayor system. Measure FF in Oakland: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Alameda County and additional election information, visit the Alameda County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Contra Costa County In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. In Richmond, residents will vote on a new mayor while voters in San Pablo will weigh in on Measure S, which would limit rent increases. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Contra Costa County and additional election information, visit the Contra Costa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Napa County California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. Measure B in Napa County: Sales tax to fund wildfire prevention and open space preservation. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Napa County and additional election information, visit the Napa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Francisco San Francisco voters will weigh in on several open seats on the county board of supervisors and board of education. Proposition A: Give mayor more power to hire and fire department heads. Proposition B: Pave way for public bank. Proposition C: Increase the city’s annual contribution to an affordable housing trust fund. Proposition D: New barriers to placing measures on the ballot. Proposition E: Changes to city contracting. Proposition G: Reopen parts of the Great Highway to vehicle traffic on weekdays. Proposition H: Parcel tax to fund Muni. Proposition J: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax California Congressional District 11: Scott Wiener and Connie Chan compete to succeed Nancy Pelosi. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Francisco and additional election information, visit the San Francisco Department of Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Mateo County Measure E in Redwood City: Limit rent increases. Measure Q in Half Moon Bay: Referendum to block proposed farmworker housing. Measure U in San Mateo County: Create independent commission to draw supervisor districts. For a complete list of San Mateo County measures and races on the ballot, visit smacre.gov/elections. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Mateo County and additional election information, visit the San Mateo County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Santa Clara County In San Jose, incumbents Peter Ortiz and Bien Doan are up for re-election in Districts 5 and 7, respectively, and there’s an open seat in District 9. Races and measures to watch in Solano County Solano County Board of Supervisors, District 4: Mike Silva and John Carli face in a runoff in a district covering Vacaville and Dixon. Measure E in Solano County: New tax on data centers and battery storage facilities in the unincorporated county areas. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Solano County and additional election information, visit the Solano County Registrar of Voters website. Races and measures to watch in Sonoma County California Congressional District 1: Mike McGuire will face James Gallagher in a seat redistricted by Proposition 50. California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. State Assembly District 12: Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward compete in a battle between business and labor. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Sonoma County and additional election information, visit the Sonoma County Registrar of Voters website. headlines.title: Preliminary 2.7 magnitude earthquake strikes near Pacifica
headlines.description: A preliminary 2.7 magnitude earthquake struck near Pacifica Wednesday evening, according to the United States Geological Survey. The quake hit at 5:17 p.m. and was centered 1.3 miles northeast of Pacifica, 3.2 miles west of San Bruno and 3.9 miles west-southwest of South San Francisco, the USGS said. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates. BAY AREA QUAKE CENTRAL Bay Area Quake Tracker, the latest earthquake stories, extensive quake prep checklists, videos and many other disaster preparedness resources all in one place: NBCBAYAREA.COM/QUAKES

headlines.title: Bonta shares resources for protecting voting ahead of Election Day
headlines.description: California Attorney General Rob Bonta is sharing informational resources with voters, judges, local election officials, and law enforcement on rules and instructions to protect voting procedures ahead of Election Day amid heightened concerns over election interference. “I know some Californians may be wondering whether everything coming out of Washington[D.C.] has changed how they can vote,” Bonta said at a briefing Wednesday in San Francisco. “Let me be clear: California’s elections are moving forward as usual … Your fundamental voting rights remain protected under California law and the rules for casting your ballots have not changed.” With Election Day next week, concerns over possible election interference have risen, especially with recent actions from the federal government. For example, the U.S. Department of Justice recently attempted to get California to set aside 20,000 mail-in ballots of voters the DOJ claimed were noncitizens. Earlier this week, a federal appeals court rejected the attempt. “Over the past year, we’ve watched the federal administration try to take control of how Americans vote, threatened to send federal law enforcement to polling places, and spread misinformation meant to make people doubt our elections, meant to sow distrust in our elections,” Bonta said. Bonta’s office has posted four notices as a resource that contain guidance on legal protections against election interference and public warnings on possible misinformation on elections being spread through different platforms. The first “publication” is a legal alert providing guidance for judges and election officials on what to do in case law enforcement tries to seize election materials pursuant to criminal search warrants. In January, the FBI used a warrant to seize ballots from an election office in Fulton County, Georgia in connection to the 2020 election. Elections Sep 17 Decision 2026 Oct 2 Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco, who also unsuccessfully ran for governor this year, seized hundreds of thousands of ballots after the state’s November 2025 special election to try to prove voter fraud. The state Supreme Court ruled that it was an illegal seizure and ordered Bianco to return the ballots. “If such a seizure occurs during the upcoming general election period, it will significantly affect the State’s ability and duty to administer the election, as well as impact Californians’ fundamental right to vote,” the alert reads. The alert seeks to provide guidance on ballot chain-of-custody requirements and recommendations for courts reviewing search warrant requests of election materials. The alert can be found at oag.ca.gov. Bonta also shared bulletins on state Senate Bill 73, which Gov. Gavin Newsom signed earlier this year. The law strengthens protections against law enforcement interfering in election procedures through intimidation or taking election materials without a court order. A bulletin providing guidance for election workers and others on SB 73 can be found at oag.ca.gov. The third bulletin is directed to all law enforcement agencies and outlines various state and federal laws pertaining to law enforcement’s limitations in conducting operations in or around polling places. It can be found at oag.ca.gov. “It is a violation of the federal government’s own federal law to have armed individuals at or near polling stations, whether it be ICE, whether it be the National Guard, whether it be other members of the military,” Bonta said. The informational resources were crafted by Bonta partly in response to rising concerns over possible immigration enforcement at polling places. Recently, there were reports of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement sightings near a polling center in Yuba City in Northern California last week. While the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that it’s “not planning operations targeting polling locations,” the agency also said it may conduct “intelligence-driven targeted enforcement” in case there is an “active public safety threat” at a polling place. Furthermore, DHS said that it will enforce against noncitizens casting ballots. “Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation,” the agency said in a statement. Lastly, Bonta sent out a notice warning the public of possible misinformation spreading related to casting ballots. He said that artificial intelligence and social media can be used to create inaccurate information about voting eligibility and intentionally mislead voters, which is illegal under state law. The notice urges voters to approach sensational or emotionally charged content related to the election with caution, and to cross-check information, especially from social media, against credible sources. The notice can be found at oag.ca.gov. If members of the public see a social media post or other information that is false or misleading about where, when or how to vote, they are encouraged to report it to the Secretary of State’s Office by emailing VoteSure@sos.ca.gov. At the briefing, Bonta urged voters to cast their ballots early, preferably at a ballot drop box or at a vote center. Vote-by-mail ballots, he said, may not arrive in time for Election Day on Tuesday if sent now. However, vote-by-mail ballots postmarked by Election Day will still be counted. Bonta said his office is prepared for any scenario that may arise in relation to election interference in the lead-up to and on Election Day. “We will be ready to deploy and roll out and address any issues that arise that threaten to interfere with your right to vote,” he said. “If you can imagine it, we are prepared for it.” Denial of voting rights can be reported in English through the Secretary of State’s confidential toll-free voter hotline at 800-345-VOTE (8683). Other language options are available at sos.ca.gov. Reports can also be made via email at elections@sos.ca.gov. For up-to-date information on how to vote, check official websites, including sos.ca.gov. Voters can register to track their ballot and confirm that it is counted at california.ballottrax.net.

headlines.title: How this private school in Palo Alto uses AI to teach students
headlines.description: A private school in Palo Alto uses AI to help students while also making sure to take the technology away. Alpha School is located right in the heart of Palo Alto and is one of the 40 Alpha Schools throughout the country. For this school, AI is on the agenda every morning, even for young kids. The school uses AI to guide students in the right direction. Each student’s lesson plan is shaped by AI to be as efficient as possible, the opposite of students packed into a classroom with one teacher. Kids study math and science for two hours a day before moving on to other social skills. “Our kids being able to get all of their academics done in the morning enables them to spend the rest of the school day building on the skills that allow for, what I would consider, true human flourishing,” Alpha School co-founder Mackenzie Price said. There’re not chatbots, just enough AI in the background to help each student on their individual learning path. “AI is there, we’re using it as a tool to optimize learning, to support and enhance and individuate learning, to serve the child, to serve the student,” dean of parents Emma Ludwick said. Even if, at a cost of $75,000 a year in tuition, that path might not lead them to a tech company. Alpha admits it’s really expensive to attend and that its idea of using ai and dividing up the day’s learning is not for everyone, but those who run the schools said they do give out financial aid and are working with public schools to share ideas.

headlines.title: Bay Area food banks, farms mobilize to better feed families in need
headlines.description: Bay Area food banks and farmers are working together to better help cash-strapped families put food on the table, especially with the holiday season approaching and ongoing cuts to food programs. On the San Mateo County coast, the owners of Brisa Ranch are busy cultivating crops for a special kind of a market place. They lead a food hub that features a collaboration between local farms and food banks. “It’s given them a turnkey opportunity to be able to know exactly what to grow in advance with knowing, ‘Hey, I want this many pallets of poblano peppers and cilantro on this date,’ for example,” Brisa Ranch co-owner Cole Mazariegos-Anastassiou said. “In turn, they’ve really been able to build their ground up with that in mind.” That’s crucial for Second Harvest of Silicon Valley and other Bay Area food banks serving a diverse community. “In our community, bok choy and cilantro are two key items that we can’t source easily on our own,” Second Harvest of Silicon Valley CEO Leslie Bacho said. “So by making these commitments to have them grow those crops and by doing it collectively with all Bay Area food banks, we’re able to do that more economically and in a way that actually supports our local food system.” The idea of connecting farms to food banks is being followed by programs being created by the California Association of Food Banks, a network of 44 food banks that work with more than 6,000 community-based organizations. “This partnership, what it’s able to do is to bring together both an investment in the food banks and also an investment in local agriculture,” California Association of Food Banks CEO Stacia Levenfeld said. Groups have had to deal with numerous funding cuts, so biopharmaceutical company Gilead Sciences this year donated $2.5 million to keep it all afloat. “We focus a lot on health,” Gilead Foundation President Jane Stafford said. “Our vision is, in fact, making better health possible. We see food and food access and food insecurity as critical to long-term health in the communities where we live and work.”

headlines.title: Will Golden State close out WNBA Finals? How to watch Valkyries vs. Dream Game 6
headlines.description: The first elimination game of the 2026 WNBA Finals is on deck. The Golden State Valkyries have a chance to close out the Finals and secure the franchise’s first championship in Game 6 against the Atlanta Dream Thursday. And there’s a chance Valkyries fans will be celebrating a championship victory at around noon PT on a weekday. That’s because the Game 6 tipoff time was moved up so it could be played at State Farm Arena, home of the NBA‘s Atlanta Hawks. Games 3 and 4 were also played at State Farm Arena, which holds around 14,000 more fans than the Dream’s normal home venue, Gateway Center Arena in College Park. But the Hawks have a game Thursday night that couldn’t be rescheduled. The Valkyries have the Dream on the ropes after winning two straight games, turning a 2-1 series deficit into a 3-2 advantage. Golden State forced Atlanta into a combined 32 turnovers across Games 4 and 5, while Kiah Stokes and Co. limited Angel Reese to 15 total points in those contests. In a matchup between two of the WNBA’s top defenses, points have been hard to come by. Atlanta is shooting 36% from the field and 24.8% from 3-point range for the series, while Golden State is at 35.2% from the field and 26.5% from deep. So, will the Dream rebound and extend the series to a decisive Game 7? Or will the Valkyries go from expansion franchise to champions in just two seasons? Here’s how to watch Game 6 of the WNBA Finals: When is the next Valkyries vs. Dream WNBA Finals game? The Valkyries and Dream will meet in Game 6 on Thursday, Oct. 29. What time does Valkyries vs. Dream Game 6 start? Tipoff from State Farm Arena is scheduled for 12:30 p.m. ET/11:30 a.m. CT/9:30 a.m. PT. WNBA Oct 16 WNBA Oct 20 What TV channel is Valkyries vs. Dream Game 6 on? Game 6 will air across USA Network, E! and SYFY. It will also be shown on Peacock. Where to stream Valkyries vs. Dream Game 6 live online Viewers can stream Game 6 on Peacock, USANetwork.com and the USA Network app. When is Valkyries vs. Dream Game 7? If Atlanta wins, Game 7 will be played Saturday, Oct. 31 at 8 p.m. ET/7 p.m. CT/5 p.m. PT. Golden State would host the winner-take-all showdown.

headlines.title: 1-year-old girl dies after being hit by vehicle in Oakland
headlines.description: A toddler died after falling out of a moving vehicle and being run over near a church and school in Oakland Tuesday afternoon. The 1-year-old girl was hit at about 3:45 p.m. in the 3700 block of Dorisa Avenue, close to the St. Paschal Baylon Catholic Church and the Northern Light School. She was taken to a hospital, where she died, according to Oakland police, who said drugs and alcohol don’t appear to have been a factor in the collision. Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee posted condolences to the child’s family on social media. “Late this afternoon, our community suffered an unimaginable tragedy with the heartbreaking loss of a one-year-old child who fell from a moving vehicle,” Lee said in her post Tuesday. “Words cannot fully express the grief we feel for the family and loved ones during this painful time. My deepest condolences and prayers are with them, as well as with our first responders. I ask everyone in our city to hold this family in their hearts tonight.” Anyone with information about the case is asked to contact the Oakland Police Department Traffic Investigation Unit at 510-777-8570.

headlines.title: ‘Her impact was boundless': Leaders pay tribute to Dolores Huerta after her death at 96
headlines.description: Renowned labor leader, civil rights icon and feminist activist Dolores Huerta has died at 96, her family announced Wednesday. Her passing prompted leaders from across the country to pen touching tributes. Read their statements below. Dolores Huerta’s family “We are deeply saddened to announce that our beloved mother, Dolores Huerta, has passed away today at the age of 96. As you can imagine, this is an incredibly difficult time for us, and we ask for privacy as we grieve this incredible loss to our family. We know that many of you around the world share in our mourning, and we will be following up on plans to recognize and celebrate her incredible life and legacy.” Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi “Today, we sadly mourn the loss of Dolores Huerta, a leader in the American labor movement and a champion for civil rights who lead with courage and determination. Dolores was a dear friend, and we all responded to her rallying cry, ‘Sí se puede,’ which inspired generations of Americans to believe in the power of collective action. I was honored to host Dolores’ birthday celebration at the United States Capitol when she turned 90, a compliment she returned to me at the California Democratic Party Convention in San Francisco earlier this year. May it be a comfort to her family and loved ones that so many mourn their loss and are praying for them at this sad time.” California Gov. Gavin Newsom and First Partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom “Dolores represented the best of us. California — and the United States — would not be what we are today without her resolute spirit, her passion for justice and fairness, and her commitment to those overlooked and forgotten. Dolores started off as a teacher, working with the children of farmworkers, and although she moved away from the classroom, she never stopped teaching. As a leader in the National Farm Workers Association, and later the United Farm Workers, she fought for gender equity, workers’ rights, and civil rights, paving the way for generations to come, and teaching people what was possible with determination and heart. She never faltered in fighting for a fairer world, continually reminding us of our shared responsibility to build a world where everyone has the respect and dignity they deserve. Because of her — and her iconic declaration, ‘Sí, se puede ’ — nothing was impossible. Dolores changed the course of history against all odds. Through protests and marches, including the Delano grape boycott, she fundamentally reshaped California as we know it. She was more than an inspiration — though she never stopped inspiring us — she was a dear friend. Her legacy lies not just in the accomplishments she achieved, but in the people who follow in her footsteps, who take up the mantle and keep creating a better world.” U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla “Angela and I mourn the passing of Dolores Huerta, a giant in the ongoing fight for workers’ rights, women’s rights, and the protection of civil liberties. She leaves behind an enduring legacy as a civil rights and labor icon who fought tirelessly for better working conditions for migrant laborers and championed the rights of immigrants and women. From the Delano Grape Strike to her work for equal pay and reproductive freedom, Dolores fought until the end for a more just and equitable future. She showed us the power of organizing, the strength of solidarity, and what we can accomplish when we stand together. Now, it’s on all of us to carry on that torch: to keep organizing and to keep fighting.” Former Vice President Kamala Harris “Dolores Huerta was a pioneering labor leader and legendary civil rights activist. Amidst the struggle of the movement, her rallying cry, “Sí se puede,” was a call to stay in the fight. The work of Dolores Huerta and the United Farm Workers was a driving force for change across California and our country. Her brilliant organizing and fierce negotiating came to the national spotlight during the Delano Grape strike, and countless people benefited from her decades-long career. Thanks to her, immigrants and workers won better wages, working conditions, environmental protections, and voting rights. I was blessed to know Dolores for many years and proud to organize alongside my dear friend to champion working families and immigrant rights. I will always be grateful for her support and friendship. We will honor her legacy by continuing the fight for the dignity of every person. Doug and I send our love and prayers to the four generations of loving family she leaves behind, the community she built, and to the millions of people who have been touched by her work.” Civil Rights 9 hours ago New Mexico Mar 19 California Attorney General Rob Bonta “Dolores Huerta was a friend, a mentor, a source of inspiration and guidance, and a lifelong hero of mine. Her activism and inspiration touched countless lives, and her ongoing legacy will surely touch countless more in the years ahead. I’m grateful she had such an influence on my own life. From my early days growing up in the headquarters of the United Farmworkers of America, to my time in public office, she was a constant, firm, irresistible force for justice and needed change. Her rallying cry “Sí Se Puede” perfectly encapsulated who she was — a woman full of fight and right who knew that if we worked together, there was nothing we couldn’t achieve. There are not enough superlatives to describe her life, legacy, and the impact she had on our nation’s ongoing pursuit of justice and fairness. She helped shape the history of the farmworkers’ movement and changed the face of the labor movement forever. She defined what it meant to own our power, use our voice, and ensure the people always remain the most potent force in our American democracy. My deepest condolences to her family. This is a devastating loss for so many in the labor movement and across the nation.” Congressman Jimmy Panetta “I am deeply saddened by the passing of Dolores Huerta, co-founder of the United Farm Workers and a pioneer in the fight for labor and civil rights, women’s rights, and equality. Her lifetime of advocacy and action helped generations of farmworkers secure better wages, safer working conditions, and a voice on the job. Dolores inspired the fight for many farmworkers to achieve the American Dream and give their children a better life. Her legacy is felt well beyond our local agricultural communities on the central coast of California and throughout our country. My heart is with her family, friends, and all those who carry forward her pursuit of giving farmworkers fairness and our children a brighter future.” Congresswoman Zoe Lofgren “I’m deeply sad to hear about the passing of Dolores Huerta, a friend and legend in the farmworkers’ movement. Her work and her vision transformed our country, especially here in her home state of California. She embodied the spirit of the movement with her phrase that will live on for generations: Sí Se Puede. May she rest in peace, and may her memory be a blessing to all who loved her.” California State Sen. Scott Wiener “Today we mourn the passing of a legend who truly changed our state and our country. Throughout her 96 years, Dolores Huerta never stopped fighting to make the world a better place. Her courage and passion helped build the farmworkers movement, and she never stopped fighting for justice — whether for workers, women, LGBTQ people, immigrants, or victims of climate disasters. She energized movements, spoke truth to power, and kept fighting until the end. I had the honor of working with Dolores on various issues, including holding Big Oil accountable for climate disasters and creating an estate tax in California. Her strength, courage, and determination continually inspired me. Rest in power, my friend.” California State Sen. Jerry McNerney “I am deeply saddened by the loss of my longtime friend and ally Dolores Huerta. She was a true American legend and fierce champion of farmworkers’ rights, women’s rights, voting rights, and social and economic justice. She will be especially missed in Stockton where she grew up and attended what is now San Joaquin Delta College. To me, she was also a trusted confidante and a steadfast partner in the fight for working families. Throughout her amazing life, she changed our world for the better, not only co-founding the farmworkers’ rights movement, but also leading the labor movement, while championing women’s rights, equality for all, economic justice and so much more. Her impact was boundless. Even after receiving the Presidential Medal of Freedom, her relentless energy continued to inspire generations to organize and stand up for justice. I was deeply proud and honored to know her and to be her friend. Her legacy and life’s work will never be forgotten, and the righteous causes she fought for will live on. Sí, se puede.” San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie “Dolores Huerta changed the lives of generations of San Franciscans and people across the country. She embodied service, dedicating her life to fighting for farmworkers’ rights, advancing civil rights, and standing up for working families. Throughout her life, she showed incredible courage, speaking out about her own experiences and standing in solidarity with other women. Her legacy will continue to inspire others—including me—and she will be deeply missed in San Francisco.” Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee “Today we lost a giant. My dear friend and sister in the struggle, Dolores Huerta, has passed away at 96. Dolores dedicated her life to justice: for farmworkers, for working families, for immigrants, and for women. Long before many others did, she understood and spoke clearly about how race, gender, and economic justice are bound together, and that we can’t win one fight without the others. She organized, she marched, she was beaten and kept going, and she never stopped believing that ordinary people, organized together, can change the world. She also knew that our vote is one of the most powerful tools we have. She registered voters, knocked on doors, and reminded every one of us that democracy only works when we show up. I will always treasure her friendship, her fierce spirit, and her wisdom. The best way we can honor her is to carry her fight forward, and that starts with casting our ballots this election. My deepest condolences to her children, her family, the Dolores Huerta Foundation, and everyone across the country and the world whose lives she touched. Rest in power, Dolores. ¡Sí se puede!”

headlines.title: WNBA Finals Game 6 watch party to be held at Thrive City in San Francisco
headlines.description: The Golden State Valkyries are one win away from being WNBA champions and will host a watch party in San Francisco on Thursday while the team plays Game 6 of the Finals in Atlanta. The Valkyries won Game 5 of the best-of-seven series 64-55 against the Atlanta Dream on Monday at Chase Center in San Francisco to go ahead 3-2 in the series and now will play Game 6 in Atlanta. Scheduling conflicts at State Farm Arena in Atlanta have prompted the WNBA to schedule Game 6 for an odd time of day on Thursday – 9:30 a.m. Pacific time, or 12:30 p.m. local time in Atlanta. The NBA’s Atlanta Hawks are moving their game there against the Cleveland Cavaliers to later Thursday night to accommodate the Valkyries-Dream game. Back in San Francisco, there will be a watch party Thursday morning at Thrive City, the plaza outside of the Chase Center arena that is home to the Valkyries and Golden State Warriors NBA team. The plaza will open to fans at 8:30 a.m. The Valkyries, founded by the same group that owns the Warriors, joined the WNBA last year and became the first expansion team in the league’s history to make the playoffs in its first season. This year, they became the first team to make the WNBA Finals in their second season. headlines.title: CSU faculty rallies continue as strike authorization vote begins
headlines.description: Rallies are taking place across California State University campuses in the Bay Area and across the state as the threat of a future strike escalates for tens of thousands of faculty members. Some rallies started before Wednesday, and almost two dozen more schools are expected to hold rallies through mid-November. Wednesday coincides with the start of a strike authorization vote for union members within the CSU system. Last week, San Jose State University union members picketed to spotlight the need for better pay so faculty and staff can keep up with a cost of living they say is a “nightmare.” Cal State East Bay also held a rally last week. San Francisco State and Sonoma State will follow Wednesday as part of almost two dozen schools that will hold rallies during the strike authorization vote period. NBC Bay Area’s Ginger Conejero Saab reports.

headlines.title: Jurors hear secret recordings in Sheng Thao corruption trial
headlines.description: Jurors heard secret recordings Wednesday in the corruption trial of former Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao. Prosecutors believe the recordings help prove that David and Andy Duong, the father-and-son co-defendants, were part of a bribery and corruption scheme involving Thao and her longtime boyfriend Andre Jones, who is also a co-defendant. Jurors heard about 40 minutes of audio from board meetings at California Waste Solutions, the company owned by the Duongs. The recordings were secretly made by Cecilia Mendez, a former employee of the company. In the recordings, businessman Mario Juarez can be heard complaining to David and Andy Duong about the mayor not keeping up her end of the bargain to buy modular housing units from Evolutionary Homes, a company Juarez helped start with the Duongs. “I think it’s disappointing she’s not keeping promises,” Juarez said. “Will be problem for her re-election.” “I have long memory and I’m pretty vengeful,” Juarez said. “There’s consequences for not keeping your end of the bargain.” Sheng Thao Oct 26 Sheng Thao Oct 23 Sheng Thao Oct 22 Sheng Thao Oct 13 Prosecutors said the Duongs helped Thao get elected. In exchange, she allegedly used her position as mayor to promise to buy housing units from the Duongs, extend their recycling contract and pay her boyfriend, Andre Jones, through a job with Evolutionary Homes. The recordings also mentioned Jones asking for more money from the company. Mendez testified that she was convicted in 2019 of acting as a real estate agent without a license, grand theft and ID theft. She also testified that the federal government granted her immunity Tuesday for secretly recording the meetings in exchange for her testimony Wednesday. During cross-examination by David Duong’s attorney, Mendez testified about her close connection with Juarez, including that they shared a daughter and remained close business partners after their separation as a couple in 2005. The defense is trying to call into question the credibility of Mendez and Juarez. Juarez has already pleaded guilty for his role in the bribery and corruption scheme and is expected to testify on behalf of the government in return for a lighter sentence.

headlines.title: New food pantry opens to support military service members and their families in the South Bay
headlines.description: A Bay Area nonprofit is expanding its efforts to combat food insecurity among military families with the opening of a new food pantry near Mountain View. The Cost of Courage Foundation celebrated the grand opening of its newest pantry Tuesday, providing another resource for active-duty service members, veterans and military families facing financial hardship. The pantry will offer groceries, personal care products and other essential items to help ease the financial burden on families who may be struggling to make ends meet. The all-volunteer nonprofit works to support those who serve and have served our country through food assistance, financial support and other programs. The new location is part of the foundation’s broader effort to address food insecurity in the military community. The organization also operates food distribution programs serving veterans and military families throughout the Bay Area and beyond.
